root.note: Early Medieval Latin rendita, built on the verb behind render (Latin reddere ‘to give back’). Wiktionary says Portuguese probably took the word through Old Catalan or Old Occitan renda.

history: If you rent a flat in Portugal, you pay a renda every month to the senhorio, the landlord. The word goes back to medieval Latin rendita, ‘what is given back, income’, from the verb that also gave Portuguese render, ‘to yield’, and rendimento, ‘income’. For the landlord the renda is income, for the tenant it is a cost: the word looks at it from the owner's side. Wiktionary thinks it probably reached Portuguese through Catalan or Occitan, where renda was already common. English rent comes from the same Latin word through French rente. In Brazil the monthly rent is usually o aluguel, and in Portugal you will also hear arrendar, ‘to let’, and contrato de arrendamento, ‘tenancy agreement’.
historyEinfach: Renda means ‘rent’, the money you pay every month for a flat. You pay it to the senhorio, the landlord. The word comes from a Latin word for ‘income’. English rent comes from the same word. In Brazil, people say aluguel for rent.

elsewhere.text: English rent and Portuguese renda are the same word, the one by way of French.
Catalan has the same form, and Portuguese probably borrowed it from there or from Occitan.
